This relatively brief gestation, when compared to other mustelids of comparable adult body mass, is likely an adaptation linked to the energetic constraints of an aquatic foraging lifestyle. By the time of weaning, the growing otter has more than tripled its birth weight, a testament to the high metabolic investment typical of this semiaquatic carnivore. The post-weaning juvenile then enters a prolonged phase of skill acquisition, learning to hunt effectively under maternal guidance before eventual dispersal.

The species' comparatively large body size relative to many other Lutrinae is thought to facilitate hunting in deeper, faster-flowing rivers. Adult females at this ultimate mass can efficiently exploit larger fish prey, reducing competition with smaller carnivores and juvenile otters. This extended sub-adult period allows for full skeletal and muscular development, ensuring that the individual can compete effectively for resources and mates. Once sexual maturity is reached, females may experience their first oestrus during the dry season, synchronizing reproductive effort with periods of high prey availability in their habitat.
